## Scene 1: Intro, Hook and Immediate Need
- **ID:** `scene-01-intro`
- **Timecode:** 0:03-0:27 (voice 23.3 s)
- **Impact point:** Why this matters: a pop-up names the app but not the command, and Apple's new controls do not change that.
- **Visual cues:** Title card with the ghost mascot. Right column reveals: a generic Mac pop-up, "What is it about to do?" marked UNKNOWN, an amber "Apple: better controls are coming / Still in beta" card, then a violet "Gatekeeper's Ward fills the gap: Today" card.

> Imagine an app on your Mac asks to see your files. Your Mac shows a pop-up that says which app is asking. But it never says what that app is about to do. A I helpers now run commands for you, so one blind click on Allow can give away your documents, your photos, even your camera. Apple is working on better controls, but the pop-up still will not show the command. Gatekeeper's Ward does, today.

## Scene 2: Baseline Flow
- **ID:** `scene-02-baseline`
- **Timecode:** 0:27-0:42 (voice 13.8 s)
- **Impact point:** Without the Ward, the user decides blind.
- **Visual cues:** Real baseline capture (`baseline_deepseek_harness_desktop_flow.mov`) beside two cards: what your Mac tells you, and what it does not (what it will run, who started it, where it runs, why it asks). Caption: "Allow or Don't Allow, and hope."

> Here is a normal Mac pop-up. An A I tool called DeepSeek Harness wants to see your Desktop folder. That is all it says. Is it just listing file names, or copying your files out? You cannot tell. So you click, and hope.

## Scene 3: Gatekeeper's Ward in Action
- **ID:** `scene-03-ward`
- **Timecode:** 0:42-1:14 (voice 30.3 s)
- **Impact point:** A small panel next to the pop-up turns a blind click into an informed choice. It only informs; the user still decides.
- **Visual cues:** Real Ward capture (`ward_deepseek_harness_desktop_flow.mov`), then the `pair.png` still. Right column reveals: what it wants (Your Desktop folder), who started it step by step, what it runs and where, warning signs (.env, .pem, id_rsa, curl, base64), then "Informs only / Never blocks".

> Now the same pop-up, with Gatekeeper's Ward running. A small panel appears right beside it. It says what the app wants. Here, your Desktop. It shows who started the request, step by step. It shows the exact command being run, and where. Now you can tell a harmless look from a data grab, and risky things, like password files, are flagged in red. The Ward never blocks anything. It just tells you. You still choose Allow or Don't Allow yourself. An informed choice, instead of a blind click.

## Scene 5: The Insight: Command Line Meets the Visual Mac
- **ID:** `scene-04a-insight`
- **Timecode:** 1:29-1:57 (voice 26.8 s)
- **Impact point:** The key idea: AI helpers work in the command line, permission pop-ups live in the visual Mac. We bring the command into the visual world without special access.
- **Visual cues:** Two cards (command line vs the visual Mac), a crimson "Command lost" gap, a "usual route" card (restricted Apple security tools) against "our route" (the Mac pauses the app that asked, so we read it live), then the banner "The command line, inside the visual Mac."

> Here is the clever part. A I helpers work in the command line, a world of plain text. Your Mac's permission pop-ups live in the visual world. The command gets lost in between. Seeing it normally needs Apple's heavy, restricted security tools, and a quick command is gone before anyone can look. But when a pop-up opens, your Mac pauses the app that asked. That pause is our chance. We bring the command line into the visual Mac, with no special access.

## Scene 6: How It Works: Zero Dark Magic
- **ID:** `scene-04-how`
- **Timecode:** 1:57-2:15 (voice 16.4 s)
- **Impact point:** Simple and safe: it runs as a normal app. No system hacks, no turning off protections.
- **Visual cues:** Four-box flow: a pop-up appears, we watch the activity log (`com.apple.TCC`), we read its command (`sysctl KERN_PROCARGS2`), we show it beside the pop-up (Fortress HUD). Then four red "No" cards: system hacks (kernel extensions), turning off protections (SIP), special Apple access, security bypasses.

> How does it work, in short? No dark magic. We watch the Mac's own activity log and wait for a permission pop-up. Then we look at the paused app and read its command. It all runs as a normal app. No system hacks, no turning off protections, and no special Apple access.
